messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ahmed, a 78-year-old Middle Eastern man, has been a roofer for over four decades. His occupation demands precision and strength, but lately, he finds himself increasingly uneasy in his daily work environment due to persistent intrusive memories and heightened anxiety stemming from a traumatic incident involving toxic chemical exposure. The event itself was sudden and severe. While working on a rooftop several months ago, Ahmed was exposed to a potent neurotoxin that had been improperly disposed of by a negligent contractor. The overwhelming fumes immediately sent him into a state of acute distress, with symptoms including nausea, disorientation, and panic. The memory of the event is still vivid in his mind, but it often surfaces involuntarily when he encounters certain triggers. Being around children has become particularly challenging for Ahmed. He finds himself reacting with alarm even to their gentle touches and can no longer relax, despite knowing that they are safe. The distress he experiences when around children stems from the memory of how helpless and vulnerable he felt during the toxic exposure. Every time he sees a child or hears news related to chemical accidents, it forces its way into his mind in fragmented and emotionally charged episodes without clear images. Ahmed’s inability to relax even in safe environments is compounded by the uncontrolled access to the traumatic memory. He often wakes up from nightmares and struggles to fall back asleep due to the overwhelming feelings of fear and panic that the memories bring. When he tries deliberately to recall what happened, it feels as if his mind goes blank, yet the emotions are intensely palpable. The distressing thoughts about being touched unexpectedly are heightened when Ahmed sees related news or encounters people who remind him of the incident. These triggers activate his memory, causing a wave of anxiety that leaves him feeling on edge and hypervigilant. The memory itself is fragmented and emotionally overwhelming, often surfacing in moments when he least expects it. Ahmed’s fear has affected not only his personal life but also his work as a roofer. He finds himself increasingly irritable and unable to concentrate during projects, which has led to conflicts with colleagues and a decline in job performance. His wife notices the changes in him and is deeply concerned about his well-being. The cumulative effect of these experiences has left Ahmed feeling isolated and overwhelmed. The memory of the toxic exposure continues to intrude on his daily life, making it difficult for him to engage fully with family and friends or perform his duties at work without being constantly vigilant. What frightens him most is that he believes he may never truly be able to escape the memory’s grip. Ahmed has decided to seek help after a particularly distressing incident where he became acutely anxious in front of his young grandson, realizing the impact this trauma was having on both himself and those around him. He hopes for relief from the intrusive memories and an ability to relax again without fear or panic. The weight of these experiences has made it clear that he needs support to navigate through this challenging period. The tightening loop of triggers, memory intrusions, and heightened anxiety is a cycle Ahmed finds increasingly difficult to break on his own. His journey towards recovery will require addressing the specific fears and memories tied to his traumatic experience while helping him regain a sense of safety and control in his daily life.
